newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asia Crude Outlook - Support emerging for MidEast.
newsitem.headline: Asia Crude Outlook - Support emerging for MidEast.

text.p: Middle East crudes, trading in Asia, appear to have found a price range after a rocky start to March trading, market sources said on Monday.
However, regional medium and heavy sweet grades, which have held premium levels as Middle East ones crashed, are set for a slide in values as trading starts to focus on March.
Weak margins, refinery run cuts and the absence of swing-buyer China are set to take their toll on the Asian market.
Shell Singapore, Esso Singapore and Singapore Refining Co have all decided to cut runs after a plunge in gas oil and fuel oil prices amid a sharp build up in stocks.

Now, South Korean refiners -- previously adverse to cutting runs -- are talking about making cuts, traders said. However, no formal announcements have been made and some traders said the refiners could just be spooking the market.
Maintaining or building domestic market share has always been the priority for South Korean refiners, so if cuts occur they could well be made across the sector, traders said.
Prices fell sharply last week but consolidated by the end of the week.
Part of the fall was sparked by Japanese refineries selling term barrels into the spot market. A crash in profit margins and refinery run cuts in Singapore exacerbated the bearish trend.
Oman dropped to MPM +6 cents after earlier trading at MPM +27/29.
One trader said he expected Oman to adopt a +10 to +15-cent range for trading from now, although another said he expected prices to hold around +10 cents.

Bangchak Petroleum Plc, in its March tender only took one Oman cargo -- at MPM +10 cents -- after receiving offers of at least four cargoes, which might cap some of Oman's potential upside, one trader said.
Murban dropped into an ADNOC +16-18 cents range from February deals of +80 cents.
However, traders said they expected just limited downside next week, although if South Korean refiners do cut it could put the grades back under pressure.
Traders said the Dubai market was firming and could help support the complex. Most Dubai crude cargoes appear to have been placed, despite India's March tender closing later this week.

Light regional grades were weakening, largely in the face of weak refining margins. However, the dramatic 20 percent plus slides in gas oil and fuel oil so far this year appeared to have bottomed out.
A major sold Tapis, one of crudes most affected by weak margins, at quotes +87 cents, sharply lower than the last deal done at +$1.75. The cargo was for first half February lifting.

Japanese and South Korean demand for medium and heavier sweet grades has supported the Indonesian market for February trading, but traders said they expected premiums to come under pressure in coming weeks as players start to focus on March trading.
"What is driving people now is that demand is lower heading into the second quarter. On top of that you've had refinery cuts," one trader said.
In addition, Japan's winter weather had been mild and temperatures are forecast to be around normal for February to April.
Traders said there is little February Indonesian trading left to be completed but they expected the benchmark Minas' premium of $1.20 to be cut back below $1.00 and possibly lower for March.
--Singapore Newsroom (+65 870 3081)
